title: The Spikes Brothers music store at 1203 Central Avenue
summary: They sold instruments, sheet music, strings and records, and took commissions on pianos and phonographs sold through Southern California Music Company.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: And that was at Central Avenue and what street?
Twelfth. 1203 Central Avenue, and that's when we started writing and publishing music.
At the music store, did you sell instruments and sheet music?

We sold instruments, sheet music and records and strings, you know, and pianos. We sold old player pianos and any other pianos we want...that we didn't have the finance to finance them but we sold for Southern California Music Company. We kept a, you know, show on the floor, and then when a customer come in and want to buy anything, then we'd take them up to Southern California, and we'd get our commission, and...because they'd sell them on ten dollars down, you know, and ten dollars a month, and we couldn't afford to do that. So we'd get our commission for the phonographs and pianos, and players was a great thing, you know, piano players, and let's see what else. Well, with big instruments, we would sell from uptown, you know-- trombones and tubas and like that band, well, it was called the Elks' Band later on, you know--the Elks Lodge--and a lot of those guys bought instruments through us. We sold them from Southern California. We'd get a...uh...

...commission, and we didn't have to carry the load of... And looking for them--half of the time and everything. But strings and records and bridges and violin bridges and picks and all that stuff we had, you know. Our biggest deal was records. See, we sold the...now, they was five or six records those days that was doing Negro music. You know, when Kate Smith...wasn't Kate, it was...
